summary: Describes the Eifel detection algorithm, which lets a TCP sender work out after the fact that it started loss recovery unnecessarily, for example after a spurious timeout. It relies on the TCP Timestamps option. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: The Eifel detection algorithm helps a TCP sender identify some cases where it started loss recovery even though the original data was not lost. It uses TCP timestamps to distinguish acknowledgments of original data from acknowledgments of retransmissions.

questions: how to detect spurious tcp retransmission
what is the eifel detection algorithm
what is a spurious timeout in tcp
how does tcp detect spurious retransmission
what is the retransmission ambiguity problem
subtitle: TCP timestamps can reveal when loss recovery began unnecessarily.

tldr.problem: After retransmitting data, a TCP sender cannot tell whether an acknowledgment responds to the original transmission or the retransmission.
tldr.mechanism: When TCP timestamps are enabled, the sender compares the timestamp echoed by the first acceptable acknowledgment with the timestamp of the retransmission. An older echoed value indicates that the acknowledgment corresponds to the original data.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines detection only. It leaves any response, such as restoring congestion-control state, to other work and is Experimental.

today: RFC 3522 is an Experimental RFC published in April 2003. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it defines detection and leaves the response algorithm outside its scope.

sections.title: The Retransmission Ambiguity
sections.content:
After a TCP retransmission, the first acceptable acknowledgment may respond to the original transmission or to the retransmission. Without extra information, the sender cannot distinguish these cases.

The Eifel algorithm uses the TCP Timestamps option to detect after the fact whether loss recovery was entered unnecessarily. It detects the condition but does not define how the sender should respond.
sections.plainLanguage: An acknowledgment may refer to the first copy of data or a later copy. Timestamps give the sender information to tell which copy the receiver acknowledged.

sections.title: Events That Can Trigger Recovery Unnecessarily
sections.content:
Packet reordering, duplication, and a sudden increase in delay can cause a sender to enter loss recovery when no data was lost. A spurious timeout is one that would not have occurred if the sender had waited longer.

These events can cause a retransmission and an unnecessary change to the sender's congestion-control state. The RFC notes that a spurious timeout can have additional effects on later transmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: A delayed or reordered packet can look like a lost packet. TCP may retransmit data and reduce its sending rate even though the original data is still on its way.

sections.title: Timestamp-Based Detection
sections.content:
When loss recovery begins, the sender records the timestamp carried by the retransmission. It then waits for the first acceptable acknowledgment and compares that acknowledgment's echoed timestamp with the saved value.

If the echoed value is smaller, it indicates that the acknowledgment was sent for an original transmission. The algorithm records that recovery was spurious, subject to checks involving DSACK and whether all outstanding data has been acknowledged.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender saves the retransmission's timestamp. If the first acknowledgment echoes an earlier timestamp, the receiver is acknowledging the original transmission, so recovery may have started unnecessarily.

sections.title: The Case Where All Acknowledgments Are Lost
sections.content:
If all acknowledgments are lost, the sender may time out even though the receiver got the data. The first later acknowledgment can echo an older timestamp, which could look like evidence of a spurious timeout.

The algorithm uses DSACK information and the acknowledgment of outstanding data to avoid treating this case as spurious. The RFC also describes how receiver timestamp behavior affects this case.
sections.plainLanguage: A timeout can be necessary when every acknowledgment disappears, even if the data arrived. The algorithm checks additional information before deciding that recovery was unnecessary.

sections.title: The Safe Variant
sections.content:
A receiver could forge echoed timestamps to make a real retransmission look unnecessary. The RFC describes a safe variant that compares the acknowledgment with the timestamp of the original transmission instead.

This variant requires the sender to retain timestamps for outstanding original data. It is more sensitive to acknowledgment loss because it depends on receiving the acknowledgment for the original transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: The safe variant checks for the exact timestamp sent with the original data. It makes forged acknowledgments harder to use, but can miss cases when acknowledgments are lost.
